meta.title: Research Summary: Why Support Search Fails on Long-Tail Questions
meta.subtitle: Evidence from retrieval evaluation, query logs, and reviewer analysis.
meta.author: Search Quality Group

executive.answer: Most long-tail failures are not caused by a single weak ranking model; they arise when query intent, document terminology, and answerable evidence are misaligned before reranking begins.
executive.scope: The analysis covers English support questions from the internal evaluation set and sampled production failures. It does not estimate the failure rate for all languages or all product areas.
implications: Improving only the reranker will leave a large share of failures unchanged.
The roadmap should prioritize query normalization, document vocabulary coverage, and evidence-quality labeling.
executive.next_action: Run a controlled experiment that combines query normalization with evidence-quality filters before changing the reranker.

metrics.label: Failures involving terminology or intent mismatch
Failures where no answerable source was indexed

items.title: Intent is lost before retrieval
items.summary: Short, context-dependent queries often omit the product object, workflow stage, or error condition needed to select the right documents.
details: Evidence: reviewer labels show repeated ambiguity in terse follow-up questions.
Consequence: lexical and vector retrieval both search the wrong semantic neighborhood.
Action: normalize the query with recent conversation entities and product context.

items.title: User vocabulary and document vocabulary diverge
items.summary: Customers describe symptoms and outcomes, while documentation is organized around feature names and implementation terms.
details: Evidence: mismatch labels account for the largest reviewed category.
Consequence: relevant documents receive weak initial retrieval scores.
Action: add terminology expansion from approved support mappings.

items.title: Some questions have no answerable indexed evidence
items.summary: A high-scoring document is not necessarily a document that contains a complete, current answer.
details: Evidence: reviewers identified missing, stale, or fragmentary sources in a material subset.
Consequence: ranking improvements can make an unanswerable result look more confident.
Action: label evidence quality and route unsupported questions to a gap workflow.

rows.mechanism: The query and indexed vocabulary do not align before reranking.
rows.intervention: Context-aware query normalization and approved terminology expansion

rows.mechanism: The index lacks a complete and current source for the question.
rows.intervention: Evidence-quality labels and a knowledge-gap workflow

rows.mechanism: Relevant evidence is retrieved but not ranked high enough.
rows.intervention: Targeted reranker training and hard-negative regression tests

items.title: Freeze the baseline
items.summary: Keep the current retriever and reranker fixed for the comparison.

items.title: Add query normalization
items.summary: Inject approved product, workflow, and terminology context.

items.title: Apply evidence-quality filters
items.summary: Separate answerable evidence from gaps and stale sources.

items.title: Measure by failure category
items.summary: Report gains and regressions separately for mismatch, evidence, and ranking failures.

items.title: Run the combined normalization and evidence-filter experiment
items.summary: Use the frozen failure set and report results by category rather than only aggregate recall.

items.title: Add answerability labels to the indexing pipeline
items.summary: Make missing, stale, and fragmentary evidence visible to retrieval and downstream generation.

sections.title: Method and limitations
sections.content: The reviewed sample combines a fixed evaluation set with selected production failures. Category shares describe the reviewed sample, not the prevalence of failures across the entire query population.
bullets: The study covers English questions only.
Reviewer labels were adjudicated for disagreements, but some intent categories remain subjective.
The analysis identifies mechanisms; it does not yet prove the expected gain from each intervention.
